The color inside a USB port can tell you quite a bit about what it does. Black ports are usually associated with USB 2.0, while blue and teal often indicate faster connections capable of transferring much larger amounts of data. Red and yellow ports typically point to charging features, including the ability to power devices while your computer is asleep.

These differences matter more than most people realize. Plugging an external SSD into an older USB port can seriously limit its transfer speed, even if the drive itself is capable of much more. Some ports also deliver more power than others, which affects how quickly connected devices charge. Two ports sitting right next to each other can have completely different capabilities.

The catch is that USB colors aren’t universally standardized. Manufacturers often follow similar conventions, but they’re free to use their own colors or ignore them entirely. That’s why a port’s color is best treated as a clue rather than a guarantee. Checking the USB symbols or actual specifications is still the most reliable way to know what your computer supports.
